title: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
summary: A spectrum from gestational hypertension to preeclampsia with severe features, eclampsia, and HELLP syndrome, defined by escalating blood pressure thresholds and end-organ findings that drive delivery timing and seizure prophylaxis decisions.
key_points: Gestational HTN: SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 on 2 readings ≥4h apart, after 20 wks, in a previously normotensive patient
Preeclampsia = gestational HTN + proteinuria (≥300mg/24h, P/C ratio ≥0.3) OR new end-organ dysfunction even without proteinuria
Severe features: BP ≥160/110, platelets <100,000, Cr >1.1 or doubled, LFTs 2x normal, pulmonary edema, new cerebral/visual symptoms
HELLP = Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets; a severe variant that can occur with minimal BP elevation
Eclampsia = new-onset tonic-clonic seizure in preeclampsia not attributable to another cause
Sustained severe-range BP (≥160/110) for ≥15 min is a hypertensive emergency requiring treatment within 30-60 min
Low-dose aspirin (81mg) started 12-28 wks (ideally <16wks) reduces risk in those at high risk for preeclampsia
management: Treat severe-range BP urgently with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine
Give magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis with severe features, and as first-line treatment for eclamptic seizures
Deliver preeclampsia without severe features/gestational HTN at ≥37 weeks
Deliver preeclampsia with severe features at ≥34 weeks after maternal stabilization
Expectant management <34 weeks only in a tertiary setting with close maternal/fetal surveillance
Deliver immediately regardless of gestational age if maternal or fetal status is unstable
Manage HELLP like severe preeclampsia; strongly consider delivery given maternal risk regardless of GA
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222, "Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia" (2020, verify current status at acog.org)
ACOG Practice Bulletin, "Chronic Hypertension in Pregnancy" (current edition — verify at acog.org)
ACOG/SMFM guidance on magnesium sulfate use in obstetrics for seizure prophylaxis

title: Postpartum Hemorrhage
summary: Defined by quantitative blood loss thresholds rather than visual estimation, with management organized around a readiness-recognition-response-reporting bundle and stage-based escalation of uterotonics and procedural interventions.
key_points: Defined as cumulative blood loss ≥1000mL, or any blood loss with signs/symptoms of hypovolemia, within 24h of birth
Quantitative blood loss measurement (graduated drapes, weighing) is preferred over visual estimation, which underestimates loss
Uterine atony causes ~70-80% of cases; recall the "4 Ts": Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin
Risk stratification (low/medium/high) should be assessed on admission and reassessed through labor
Response is organized in escalating stages from prevention through massive hemorrhage protocols
Early, multidisciplinary team activation improves outcomes more than any single medication
management: Give prophylactic oxytocin to all patients as active management of the third stage
First-line for atony: uterine massage plus oxytocin; add second-line uterotonics (methylergonovine, carboprost, misoprostol) if bleeding continues
Give tranexamic acid 1g IV within 3 hours of hemorrhage onset; repeat once if bleeding persists
Escalate to intrauterine balloon tamponade or compression sutures for refractory atony
Activate massive transfusion protocol and call for additional help early, not after decompensation
Consider uterine artery embolization or ligation, and hysterectomy for life-threatening refractory hemorrhage
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 183, "Postpartum Hemorrhage" (2017, verify current status at acog.org)
ACOG Committee Opinion No. 794, "Quantitative Blood Loss in Obstetric Hemorrhage" (2019)
Council on Patient Safety in Women's Health Care / AIM Obstetric Hemorrhage Patient Safety Bundle (current edition — verify at saferbirth.org)

title: Preterm Labor and Preterm Birth Prevention
summary: Covers diagnosis of preterm labor and the evidence-based toolkit to improve neonatal outcomes — short-course tocolysis, antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium for neuroprotection, and progesterone for recurrence prevention — now reflecting the 2023 withdrawal of 17-OHPC.
key_points: Preterm labor = regular contractions with cervical change before 37 0/7 weeks
Antenatal corticosteroids recommended 24 0/7-33 6/7 wks, and considered 34 0/7-36 6/7 wks, if delivery risk within 7 days
In the periviable window (22-25 6/7 wks), corticosteroids may be considered at 23 0/7-23 6/7 wks after counseling if resuscitation is planned
Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is used <32 weeks when delivery is anticipated within 24 hours
Tocolysis (nifedipine, indomethacin) is short-term (~48h) to allow steroid/magnesium administration or transport, not indefinite pregnancy prolongation
Vaginal progesterone is recommended for singleton pregnancy with a short cervix (≤25mm before 24 weeks)
17-alpha hydroxyprogesterone caproate (Makena) was withdrawn from the US market in April 2023 for lack of efficacy
management: Confirm diagnosis with cervical exam; fetal fibronectin or cervical length can help rule out preterm labor when exam is equivocal
Give a single course of antenatal corticosteroids if gestational age and delivery risk criteria are met
Start short-course tocolysis (indomethacin <32wk, or nifedipine) to permit steroid/magnesium administration and transport
Give magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if <32 weeks and delivery is imminent
Avoid prolonging tocolysis beyond 48 hours; it does not improve neonatal outcomes used long-term
Consider a single rescue course of corticosteroids if ≥14 days since the first course and new risk of delivery within 7 days, <34 weeks
Discontinue any ongoing 17-OHPC and discuss vaginal progesterone as the evidence-based alternative when indicated
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin, "Management of Preterm Labor" (current edition — verify at acog.org)
ACOG/SMFM Practice Advisory, "Use of Antenatal Corticosteroids at 22 Weeks of Gestation" (2021)
SMFM Statement, response to FDA withdrawal of 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate (2023)
ACOG/SMFM guidance on magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection before anticipated preterm birth (current edition — verify at acog.org)

title: PPROM and Term PROM Management
summary: Management balances infection and abruption risk against prematurity, generally favoring expectant management for PPROM between 24-33 6/7 weeks and delivery at or beyond 34 weeks or at term.
key_points: Diagnosis relies on pooling, ferning, and nitrazine-positive fluid, supported by ultrasound oligohydramnios
PPROM = membrane rupture before 37 weeks; term PROM = rupture at ≥37 weeks before labor begins
Latency to delivery is generally longer the earlier the gestational age at rupture
Major risks of PPROM: chorioamnionitis, placental abruption, cord compression/prolapse, and preterm birth
Expectant management is generally recommended 24-33 6/7 weeks absent a contraindication
Most patients with term PROM labor spontaneously within 24 hours of rupture
management: Confirm gestational age, rule out infection, abruption, or nonreassuring fetal status, and assess fetal presentation
For PPROM 24-33 6/7 wks: admit, give latency antibiotics (ampicillin/azithromycin-based regimen), a single corticosteroid course, and GBS prophylaxis at delivery
Give magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if <32 weeks and delivery is imminent
Monitor daily for infection, abruption, or labor; deliver promptly for chorioamnionitis, abruption, or nonreassuring status
Proceed to delivery at 34 0/7 weeks rather than continued expectant management
For term PROM, offer immediate induction (reduces infection risk) versus a limited period of expectant management with GBS prophylaxis as indicated
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 217, "Prelabor Rupture of Membranes" (2020, verify current status at acog.org)

title: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
summary: Universal screening at 24-28 weeks using either a one-step or two-step approach, with management stepping from lifestyle therapy to insulin and delivery timing individualized by glycemic control.
key_points: Universal screening at 24-28 weeks; ACOG accepts either a one-step 75g 2h OGTT or a two-step 50g GLT followed by 100g 3h OGTT
Two-step diagnostic (Carpenter-Coustan): fasting ≥95, 1h ≥180, 2h ≥155, 3h ≥140 mg/dL; ≥2 abnormal values = GDM
One-step (IADPSG) diagnostic: fasting ≥92, 1h ≥180, or 2h ≥153 mg/dL; any single abnormal value = GDM
Early pregnancy screening is recommended for patients with risk factors (obesity, prior GDM, PCOS, family history) to detect pre-existing diabetes
A1GDM = diet-controlled; A2GDM = requires medication
Key complications: fetal macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycemia, and future maternal type 2 diabetes risk
management: First-line therapy: medical nutrition therapy, carbohydrate counting, exercise, and self blood-glucose monitoring
Glycemic targets: fasting <95 mg/dL, 1h postprandial <140 mg/dL, 2h postprandial <120 mg/dL
If lifestyle measures fail to reach targets, insulin is first-line pharmacotherapy; metformin or glyburide are alternatives
Initiate antenatal fetal surveillance for A2GDM or when additional risk factors are present
Deliver well-controlled A1GDM at 39-40 6/7 weeks and well-controlled A2GDM at 39-39 6/7 weeks; deliver earlier if poorly controlled
Screen for persistent diabetes postpartum with a 75g 2h OGTT at 4-12 weeks, and counsel on lifelong type 2 diabetes risk
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 190, "Gestational Diabetes Mellitus" (2018, verify current status at acog.org)
ACOG Clinical Practice Update, "Screening for Gestational and Pregestational Diabetes in Pregnancy and Postpartum" (2024)

title: Shoulder Dystocia
summary: An unpredictable obstetric emergency requiring a stepwise maneuver sequence beginning with McRoberts positioning, with meticulous post-delivery documentation to support later review.
key_points: Defined as delivery requiring additional maneuvers beyond gentle downward traction to deliver the fetal shoulders
Risk factors include macrosomia, maternal diabetes/GDM, prior shoulder dystocia, and operative vaginal delivery
Most cases occur without identifiable risk factors and are not reliably predictable or preventable
The "turtle sign" (head retraction against the perineum) is the classic presenting finding
Key complications: brachial plexus injury (usually transient), clavicle or humerus fracture, hypoxic injury, and maternal trauma/PPH
Fundal pressure and excessive head traction are associated with neurologic injury and should be avoided
management: Call for additional help immediately (obstetric, nursing, anesthesia, pediatric support) and note the time of head delivery
Perform McRoberts maneuver (maternal hip hyperflexion) first — often sufficient alone
Apply suprapubic pressure in conjunction with McRoberts
If unsuccessful, proceed to internal rotational maneuvers (Rubin, Woods screw) or delivery of the posterior arm
Consider additional maneuvers such as the all-fours (Gaskin) position; episiotomy may aid access but does not relieve bony impaction
Document thoroughly afterward: time of head and body delivery, maneuvers used and sequence, personnel present, and infant condition
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 178, "Shoulder Dystocia" (2017, verify current status at acog.org)
